tips.title: The preposition belongs to the noun
tips.body: Learn the place **with** its preposition: **à la** campagne, **à la** montagne, **au** bord de la mer, **en** ville, **dans un** village, **dans le** nord, **dans l'** ouest. Guessing the preposition separately is how the mark is lost.

tips.title: Il fait takes an adjective only
tips.body: *Il fait* goes with **adjectives**: *il fait chaud, froid, beau*. **Il pleut** and **il neige** are complete verbs and never take *il fait*. Windy and foggy use **il y a du vent / du brouillard**.

tips.title: Test the fraction against the number
tips.body: Before choosing *la moitié*, *un tiers* or *un quart*, check it against the figure: half is 50%, a third about 33%, a quarter 25%. A question will offer all three and only one will be true of the number in front of you.

tips.title: One idea developed beats three adjectives
tips.body: *Calme et jolie et propre* is one idea three times. *Calme parce qu'il n'y a pas beaucoup de circulation, **ce qui est** agréable* is one idea developed twice, and scores far higher. Add a tense other than the present and you are in the top band.

steps.title: Où j'habite
steps.body: Describing where you live starts with two verbs that do most of the work. - **se trouver** — to be located: *Ma ville **se trouve** dans le nord de la France.* - **se situer** — to be situated: *Le village **se situe** près de la montagne.* Both are reflexive, so they need **se**, and both take **dans**, **près de**, **à** or **au bord de** for the place. The compass points take **dans le** and no capital letter: > *dans le **nord**, dans le **sud, dans l'est, dans l'ouest*** Note *dans l'est* and *dans l'ouest*: the vowel takes an apostrophe. For the kind of place, the preposition changes with the noun and has to be learnt with it: - **à la** campagne, **à la** montagne - **au** bord de la mer - **en** ville, **en** banlieue - **dans un** village, **dans une** grande ville

steps.title: Le paysage
steps.body:
Once you have said **where**, say **what it looks like**. A description that names two or three features scores far better than *c'est joli*.

Useful nouns come in pairs of gender you have to know:

- **la** montagne, **la** forêt, **la** rivière, **la** mer, **la** campagne
- **le** fleuve, **le** lac, **le** champ, **le** village, **le** paysage

And the sentence pattern that carries most descriptions:

> *Il y a des montagnes et beaucoup de forêts.*
> *Le paysage est vert et très calme.*

**Beaucoup de** never takes *des*: it is *beaucoup **de** forêts*, never *beaucoup des forêts*.

To add detail without new vocabulary, use an adjective plus an intensifier: *assez* (quite), *très* (very), *vraiment* (really), *trop* (too). Remember the adjective agrees: *une forêt **verte***, *des champs **verts***.

rows: Il y a des forêts vertes.
Il y a des montagnes et beaucoup de forêts.
Le paysage est vraiment calme, ce que j'adore.

check.solution: **Beaucoup de** never becomes *beaucoup des*. The same is true of *peu de*, *trop de* and *assez de*.

steps.title: Le climat et le temps
steps.body:
French separates two ideas that English often blurs.

- **Le climat** is what the weather is **usually** like: *Le climat est doux.*
- **Le temps** is the weather **now**: *Aujourd'hui, il fait beau.*

Weather expressions mostly use **il fait** plus an adjective, but three common ones do not, and those are the ones people get wrong:

- *il **pleut*** — it is raining (from *pleuvoir*)
- *il **neige*** — it is snowing
- *il y a **du vent** / **du brouillard** / **des orages*** — it is windy / foggy / stormy

So *il fait pleut* is wrong: *pleuvoir* is already a verb.

For the climate, the adjectives worth having are **doux** (mild), **humide** (damp), **sec** (dry), **tempéré** (temperate), **rude** (harsh). Note *sec* becomes **sèche** in the feminine.

words.note: a verb on its own, never il fait pleut

steps.title: Comparer deux endroits
steps.body: Comparisons are worth learning properly because they turn two facts into one better sentence, and they appear constantly in infographic questions. - **plus ... que** — more ... than: *Il fait **plus** chaud **que** dans le nord.* - **moins ... que** — less ... than: *Il pleut moins qu'en Bretagne.* - **aussi ... que** — as ... as: *C'est **aussi** calme qu'à la campagne.* The adjective in the middle still **agrees** with what it describes: *Ma ville est **plus polluée que** la tienne.* Two irregulars to know: - *bon* → **meilleur** (better), not *plus bon* - *bien* → **mieux** (better, of doing something) For the most or the least, add the article: *le climat **le plus** doux*, *la région **la moins** peuplée*.

steps.note: start from what you want to compare

steps.text: *Dans le sud, il fait **plus chaud que** chez moi.*
To go the other way: *Chez moi, il fait **moins chaud que** dans le sud.*
For a superlative: *Le sud a **le climat le plus** chaud de la France.*

steps.title: Lire une infographie
steps.body:
Infographics turn up in reading papers because they pack a lot of information into few words. The French you need is mostly **numbers plus one verb**.

Fractions and proportions:

- **la moitié** — half
- **un tiers** — a third
- **un quart** — a quarter
- **41 pour cent** — 41 per cent
- **la plupart** — most

Verbs for what the numbers do:

- **augmenter** — to increase
- **diminuer**, **baisser** — to decrease, to fall
- **rester stable** — to stay the same

And the phrase that introduces a figure: **selon cette enquête** — according to this survey.

The skill is matching a **word** to a **number**. If the graphic says 34%, then *plus d'un tiers* is true, *la moitié* is false, and *la plupart* is false. A question will usually offer you all three.

steps.title: À toi : décris ta région
steps.body:
**Partie A.** Réponds en français, en phrases complètes.

1. Où se trouve ta ville ou ton village ?
2. Comment est le paysage ? Nomme deux choses.
3. Comment est le climat ? Donne deux détails.

**Partie B.** Regarde l'infographie de l'étape 5.

4. Quel moyen de transport est le moins utilisé ? Écris une phrase complète.
5. Compare le vélo et le bus avec *plus … que* ou *moins … que*.

**Partie C.** Écris trois phrases comparant ta région avec une autre région que tu connais. Utilise *plus … que*, *moins … que* et *aussi … que*, une fois chacun.

For part 5, check the two figures before you choose which comparative to use.

check.solution: Le vélo est à 34% et le bus à 17%, donc **on utilise le vélo plus que le bus**. La voiture, à 41%, reste le premier moyen de transport.

options: On utilise le bus plus que le vélo.
On utilise le vélo autant que le bus.

steps.title: Aller plus loin: du détail, pas des adjectifs
steps.body:
Two habits separate a top answer from a competent one here, and neither needs rare vocabulary.

**First: give a reason or a consequence, not another adjective.** Compare:

> *Ma ville est calme et jolie et propre.* — three adjectives, one idea.
> *Ma ville est très calme **parce qu'il n'y a pas beaucoup de circulation**, ce qui est agréable **quand on veut dormir**.* — one adjective, developed twice.

The second is shorter in ideas and far longer in credit, because it shows a **subordinate clause** and a **reason**.

**Second: use a tense other than the present.** Any description can carry one without strain:

> *Avant, il y **avait** une forêt ici, mais elle **a été coupée**.* — imperfect plus a perfect passive.
> *L'année prochaine, on **construira** une piste cyclable.* — future.

A description written entirely in the present caps at the middle band however accurate it is.

**A caution about the climate.** Be careful with *le climat change* versus *le temps change*. *Le temps change* means the weather is changing today, which is trivial. **Le climat change** means the climate is changing, which is the thing worth writing about. Using the wrong one turns a serious sentence into a remark about an afternoon.

And a small accuracy point examiners notice: **il y a** has no *s* on *a*, and *il y a* is used for *there is* **and** *there are*. *Il y ont* does not exist.

Ma ville est calme parce qu'il n'y a pas beaucoup de circulation.

… ce qui est agréable quand on veut dormir.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- **se trouver** and **se situer** for where a place is, both reflexive.
- Compass points: **dans le nord / sud**, **dans l'est / l'ouest**, no capital letters.
- The preposition belongs to the noun: **à la** campagne, **au** bord de la mer, **en** ville, **dans un** village.
- **beaucoup de**, never *beaucoup des*.
- **Le temps** is the weather now; **le climat** is what it is usually like.
- *Il fait* takes an **adjective**; **il pleut** and **il neige** are verbs on their own; **il y a du vent**.
- **sec** becomes **sèche** in the feminine.
- Comparatives: **plus / moins / aussi … que**, with the adjective still agreeing. *Que* becomes *qu'* before a vowel.
- **bon** becomes **meilleur**, not *plus bon*.
- Infographics: **la moitié** 50%, **un tiers** about 33%, **un quart** 25%, **la plupart** most.
- **augmenter**, **diminuer**, **baisser**, **rester stable** for what a figure does.
- Develop one idea with **parce que** and **ce qui est** rather than listing adjectives.
- Get at least one tense other than the present into any description.

questions.modelAnswer: **Modèle.** > *Ma ville **se trouve dans le nord-ouest** de l'Angleterre, assez près de la mer. Le paysage est très vert, avec **beaucoup de** collines et de champs autour du village. **Le climat est doux mais humide**, et en hiver **il pleut** presque tous les jours, **ce que je trouve** un peu déprimant. **Avant, il y avait** une vieille forêt derrière chez moi, mais elle **a été coupée** il y a deux ans. **L'année prochaine, on plantera** de nouveaux arbres dans le parc, et j'espère que ce sera plus joli qu'aujourd'hui.* **What earns the marks.** *Se trouve dans le nord-ouest* for location. *Beaucoup de*, not *des*. The climate and the weather kept separate. Four tenses: present, **imperfect** (*il y avait*), **perfect passive** (*a été coupée*), **future** (*on plantera*). And two opinions, each with a reason.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Modèle.**

> *Selon cette enquête, la voiture est le moyen de transport **le plus utilisé**, avec 41 pour cent des élèves. **Plus d'un tiers** des élèves viennent à vélo, ce qui est encourageant. On utilise le vélo **beaucoup plus que** le bus, qui n'est choisi que par 17 pour cent. **Le moins populaire** est la marche, car seulement 8 pour cent des élèves viennent à pied.*

**Check the words against the numbers.** *Plus d'un tiers* is true of 34%, since a third is about 33%. *La moitié* would be false. The comparative *plus que* is right because 34 is greater than 17.

examTechnique.body:
For a description, answer the three questions the examiner is really asking: **where** it is, **what it looks like**, and **what you think of it**. A description with no opinion cannot reach the top band.

Use *se trouver* or *se situer* and get the preposition right. Learn each place with its preposition rather than choosing one at the time.

Keep *le temps* and *le climat* apart. A question about the climate wants what it is **usually** like.

For an infographic, read the number first and then test the French word against it. Only one of *la moitié*, *un tiers* and *un quart* will be true.

In writing, develop one idea with *parce que* and *ce qui est* instead of adding another adjective, and make sure at least one sentence is not in the present tense.

Check agreements at the end, particularly on adjectives after a feminine noun.
examinerErrors: Writing *beaucoup des forêts* instead of *beaucoup de forêts*.
Writing *il fait pleut*, when *pleuvoir* is already a verb.
Using the wrong preposition: *en campagne* instead of *à la campagne*.
Capitalising the compass points, which French does not do.
Choosing *la moitié* for a figure that is not close to 50%.
Describing everything in the present tense, which caps the band.
Listing adjectives instead of developing one idea with a reason.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer names specific features rather than reaching for *joli* and *sympa*, and it develops each one with a reason or a consequence so the description reads as a paragraph rather than a list. It moves between tenses without being asked, saying what used to be there and what will change. Reading an infographic, it tests each proportion word against the actual figure rather than picking the one it recognises, and it turns two figures into a comparison. It keeps *le temps* and *le climat* distinct, knowing that one is about this afternoon and the other about something worth writing about.
